clue.text: Don't sit on your arse and quit life!

parts.note: the order to rise from your seat
taken as written
to quit a place is to go

explanation.surface: A rude exhortation to stop lounging around, followed by a grim one to end it all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quit life' reads as a suicidal instruction; in fact 'life' alone is the definition, in the sense of vigour.
explanation.definitionFit: Life in the sense of liveliness or energy is what the idiom for drive and vitality describes.

clue.text: On getting an erection, be dirty

indicators.note: in a down entry, something erected stands upright, so the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to be is to exist, to live

explanation.surface: A smutty remark that arousal makes one behave filthily.
explanation.definitionFit: Dirty in the moral sense of wicked or depraved is a looser synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Woody has change of political allegiance when a choice is to be made

definitions.text: when a choice is to be made

indicators.note: switching political sides means a letter standing for Right is swapped for one standing for Left

parts.note: a woody is slang for a stiffy

explanation.surface: Someone called Woody defects to another party just as the country goes to the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: Woody looks like a name (Woody Allen, perhaps); it is slang. R for right becomes L for left, giving ELECTION.
explanation.definitionFit: A vote is held precisely at the time when the public must pick between candidates.

clue.text: Goody-goody found in the City area? A fable!

indicators.note: something found within another thing sits inside it

parts.note: EC is the postcode district covering the City of London
PI, short for pious, is a crossword goody-goody

explanation.surface: Asking whether a virtuous banker in the Square Mile is a mere fairy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district; finding a goody-goody there is the fable.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a long heroic narrative, loosely a legend or fabled story.

clue.text: Supposed guardians of the peace sticking one in balls — humourless, lousy things

indicators.note: sticking something in another puts it inside that other thing

parts.note: balls and rot both mean nonsense
the Roman numeral for one
as in po-faced, solemn and humourless
lice are what make a head lousy

explanation.surface: A sour description of officers who supposedly keep order by kneeing people in the groin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supposed' is the satirist's sneer: squads in riot gear are meant to keep the peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Officers equipped to control disorderly crowds are, in principle, protectors of public order.

clue.text: Scumbag's second success

parts.note: the abbreviation for second
a hit is a success

explanation.surface: A villain enjoying another triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are vulgar terms of abuse for a contemptible person.

clue.text: A lot of bitterness against pole dancing cover

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and land in a new order
a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter goes

parts.note: envy, with its last letter dropped
the word pole, rearranged

explanation.surface: A resentful onlooker set against a pole dancer and her skimpy costume.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop is to wrap up or surround, a verb synonym of cover.

clue.text: Bad-mouth Slim

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to insult or snub

explanation.walkthrough: Slim looks like a nickname being insulted; it is an adjective, and bad-mouth a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for snubbing or disparaging, and an adjective for slender or slight in build.

clue.text: Hardly satisfying read, Telegraph's leader

parts.note: to scan a text is to read it

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the newspaper's name

explanation.surface: A sniffy review of the Daily Telegraph's editorial as an unrewarding read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader' suggests a newspaper editorial; here it only means the first letter. The Telegraph is a British broadsheet.
explanation.definitionFit: Scant means barely enough, so an amount that hardly satisfies is insufficient.

clue.text: (& 16ac.) As broken up by dominant police brutes, justice ultimately lacking?

definitions.text: As broken up by dominant police brutes, justice ultimately lacking?

indicators.note: something broken up is smashed into pieces that can be reassembled differently
ultimately points at the final letter of the word before it, the one to drop
lacking means without, so the selected letter is taken away from the rest

parts.note: the fodder, twenty letters taken as written
the final letter of justice, which is removed

explanation.surface: A protest being violently broken up by heavy-handed officers, with no justice in sight.
explanation.walkthrough: One E is removed from the three fodder words, then the remaining nineteen letters are rearranged; the whole clue also describes what happens to a protest at the hands of brutal police.
explanation.definitionFit: A protest march or rally in the street is exactly what heavy-handed police are said to break up.

clue.text: Purity boobs, backing into yachtsman

indicators.note: putting one thing into another places it inside

parts.note: Chay Blyth, the British round-the-world yachtsman

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: slang for breasts

explanation.surface: A smutty headline about breasts and a sailor, oddly labelled purity.
explanation.walkthrough: Chay Blyth was the first person to sail single-handed westward round the world; his first name is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Chastity is sexual abstinence, hence moral purity, an abstract-noun synonym.

clue.text: An unconventional atrocity

parts.note: surface reading: an outrage of an unusual or novel kind
setter's reading: an outrage that breaks the Geneva Conventions on the conduct of armed conflict

explanation.walkthrough: Unconventional normally means unusual; here it means contrary to the Geneva Conventions governing the treatment of prisoners and civilians.
explanation.definitionFit: Atrocities in armed conflict that breach international conventions are prosecuted under exactly this name.

clue.text: Yobs possibly making stand-ups experience drugs

parts.note: stand-up comedians are comics
to trip is to be high on hallucinogens

explanation.surface: Louts turning comedians into drug-takers.
explanation.walkthrough: Yobs was a long-running cartoon strip by Tony Husband in Private Eye, the magazine this puzzle appears in; a yob is a British lout.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is an example: Yobs is a recurring cartoon series in Private Eye.

clue.text: In the grip of dysentery? Join the competition!

parts.note: the letters run consecutively inside this word

explanation.surface: Someone suffering from the runs is invited to take part in a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a race or contest is to sign up and take part in it.

clue.text: Prize the end of Jeremy Thorpe, maybe? No way

indicators.note: maybe hints that the letters are a possible rearrangement rather than fixed
no means without, so the letter standing for a direction is dropped
the end of a word is its final letter, which is joined on here

parts.note: the surname as written
east is a compass way, E
the final letter of the first name

explanation.surface: Asking whether the downfall of Jeremy Thorpe was a coup for someone, then rejecting it.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Thorpe was a Liberal Party leader brought down by scandal in the 1970s. Drop E from his surname, add Y, then rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy is a cup or award presented to the winner, a synonym for prize.

clue.text: see19dn.
see 9ac.

parts.note: lone and single both mean solitary

explanation.definitionFit: Capone was the notorious Chicago gangster of the Prohibition era, an example of a mobster.

clue.text: Football smack-artist by the sound of it

parts.note: someone who socks, or punches, people

clue.text: (& 15dn.) What to call ministers of a certain political persuasion not involved in sleaze, etc?

parts.note: the right wing of politics
decent and upright, untainted by scandal

explanation.surface: Wondering how to address clean Conservative ministers, if any exist.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark carries the satire: Tory ministers in the 1990s sleaze era were seldom honourable. Privy Counsellors, including Cabinet ministers, are styled the Right Honourable.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the formal title used for British Privy Counsellors, which includes senior government ministers.

clue.text: Burst into laughter: Clegg's introduction has gone and accumulated points!

explanation.walkthrough: Nick Clegg was leader of the Liberal Democrats; 'introduction' means only his initial.
explanation.definitionFit: To rack up a score is an idiom for amassing points or wins steadily.

clue.text: "Prison child's play with no aggravation": US department

a playground chasing game
the word no, jumbled

explanation.definitionFit: The Pentagon is the headquarters of the US Department of Defense, and by metonymy the department itself.

clue.text: Close to clipping wings of lady's man
